# Problem 1

```{r}
data("ny_noaa")

glimpse(ny_noaa)

ny_noaa |>
  summarize(
    observations = n(),
    stations = n_distinct(id),
    first_date = min(date),
    last_date = max(date)
  ) |>
  knitr::kable()

ny_noaa |>
  summarize(
    across(
      everything(),
      ~ mean(is.na(.x)) * 100
    )
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(
    everything(),
    names_to = "Variable",
    values_to = "Missing (%)"
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2)
```
This dataset contains `r nrow(ny_noaa)` observations and `r ncol(ny_noaa)` variables, representing daily weather records from `r dplyr::n_distinct(ny_noaa$id)` stations in NY state between `r min(ny_noaa$date)` and `r max(ny_noaa$date)`. Each row represents a station-day record. 

Variables include station ID, date, precipitation, snowfall, snow depth, and daily maximum and minimum temperatures.

Missingness varies substantially across variables. Precipitation is missing in 5.62% of observations, snowfall in 14.69%, and snow depth in 22.80%. Both maximum and minimum temperatures are missing in approximately 43.71% of observations. Temperature analyses therefore rely on a substantially reduced subset of the records. Station ID and date have no missing values.

## Data cleaning

```{r}
noaa_clean =
  ny_noaa |>
  separate(
    date,
    into = c("year", "month", "day"),
    sep = "-",
    convert = TRUE,
    remove = FALSE
  ) |>
  mutate(
    tmax = as.numeric(tmax) / 10,
    tmin = as.numeric(tmin) / 10,
    prcp = prcp / 10
  )

noaa_clean |>
  filter(!is.na(snow)) |>
  count(snow, sort = TRUE) |>
  slice_head(n = 10) |>
  knitr::kable(
    col.names = c("snowfall (mm)", "number of observations")
  )
```

The date was separated into year, month, and day while retaining the original date variable. Maximum and minimum temperatures were converted to numeric values and expressed in degrees Celsius. Precipitation was converted to millimeters; snowfall and snow depth were already recorded in millimeters.

The most frequently observed snowfall value is 0 mm (2,008,508 observations), followed by 25 mm (31,022), 13 mm (23,095), and 51 mm (18,274). Zero dominates because most station-days have no snowfall. Common positive values such as 13, 25, 51, and 76 mm are approximately equivalent to 0.5, 1, 2, and 3 inches, suggesting that the recorded values reflect conversion and rounding from measurements in inches.## Average maximum temperature in January and July

## average max temperature in January and July
```{r}
noaa_monthly =
  noaa_clean |>
  filter(month %in% c(1, 7)) |>
  group_by(id, year, month) |>
  summarize(
    observed_days = sum(!is.na(tmax)),
    mean_tmax = mean(tmax, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  filter(observed_days > 0) |>
  mutate(
    month = factor(
      month,
      levels = c(1, 7),
      labels = c("January", "July")
    )
  )

ggplot(noaa_monthly, aes(x = year, y = mean_tmax)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.25, size = 0.8, color = "#2C7FB8") +
  facet_wrap(~ month, nrow = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "Average daily maximum temperature by station and year",
    subtitle = "Each point represents one station in one year",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Mean daily maximum temperature (°C)",
    caption = "Means use available daily observations; station-months with no data are excluded."
  ) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 13),
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold")
  )
```
July has much higher average daily maximum temperatures than January. Most station-level averages fall around 20–33°C in July and −10–10°C in January. Temperatures vary across stations, and many stations show similar year-to-year fluctuations, suggesting shared regional weather patterns. January shows more pronounced interannual variation than July.

There are several unusually low station-level averages, including a July value near 14°C around 1988. These observations warrant checking the underlying daily records and the number of observed days. Because monthly means use available observations, incomplete coverage may affect their comparability. The figure alone does not establish a clear long-term trend.

## Temperature relationship and snowfall distributions

```{r, fig.width=12, fig.height=6}
temperature_plot =
  noaa_clean |>
  filter(!is.na(tmin), !is.na(tmax)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = tmin, y = tmax)) +
  geom_bin_2d(bins = 70) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(
    trans = "log10",
    name = "Count"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Daily maximum vs. minimum temperature",
    x = "Minimum temperature (°C)",
    y = "Maximum temperature (°C)"
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

snowfall_plot =
  noaa_clean |>
  filter(snow > 0, snow < 100) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = factor(year), y = snow)) +
  geom_boxplot(
    fill = "#A6CEE3",
    outlier.alpha = 0.2,
    outlier.size = 0.5
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Annual snowfall distributions",
    subtitle = "Only station-days with 0 < snowfall < 100 mm",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Snowfall (mm)"
  ) +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(
      angle = 90,
      hjust = 1,
      vjust = 0.5,
      size = 8
    )
  )

(temperature_plot + snowfall_plot) +
  plot_layout(widths = c(1, 1.2)) +
  plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A")
```

Daily maximum and minimum temperatures show a strong positive association: days with higher minimum temperatures generally also have higher maximum temperatures. 

Most observations lie within a concentrated diagonal band. A few isolated records have extreme temperatures or maximum temperatures below minimum temperatures; these warrant further investigation rather than automatic removal.

Among station-days with snowfall greater than 0 and less than 100 mm, the annual distributions are broadly similar. Median snowfall is approximately 25 mm across years, and the middle 50% of observations generally spans about 13–51 mm. Some years, such as 2006 and 2010, have lower upper quartiles. These conditional distributions do not describe annual total snowfall or the frequency of snowfall days.
